opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. The way I see it, foundation models today are built on the senses we've already digitized. We have cameras and microphones, we have massive corpora of text and images and audio, and so models learned to see and hear because the data was there. Smell never got that treatment. There's no "JPEG for odor," no standardized way to capture a scent, store it, and play it back. So the first step is building the representation, a map of odor space.

That's a lot of what we worked on, first at Google Research and now at Osmo. We trained graph neural networks on molecular structure to predict what a molecule smells like, and we got to the point where the model's predictions matched a trained human panel about as well as individual panelists match each other. Out of that comes a principal odor map, an embedding space where molecules that smell alike sit near each other, even when they look very different chemically. That embedding is the foundation. It's the analog of what ImageNet-era representations did for vision.

Once you have it, smell can become one more modality in the bigger models. Picture a multimodal model that can link the word "petrichor" or "fresh-cut grass" to a region of odor space, connect that to the molecules that produce it, and reason about it alongside text and images. Then you need the I/O. On the input side, sensors that can read a complex mixture in the air and map it into that space. On the output side, formulation, meaning you go from a target point in odor space to a physical recipe you can actually make. Reading, mapping, and writing smell is what closes the loop.

There are real hard problems left. Mixtures are much harder than single molecules because odors interact nonlinearly. Perception varies across people, and context and concentration matter enormously. And the data is still tiny next to what we have for vision or language, so a lot of the work is just carefully generating high-quality labeled data with trained panels.

But I'm optimistic, because the payoff is huge. Smell sits right next to health. Diseases change the volatile compounds our bodies give off, and dogs can detect some cancers. If machines can smell reliably, you get early diagnostics, food safety, environmental monitoring, and even better insect repellents, which matters for diseases like malaria. So for me, building smell into foundation models isn't a novelty. It's giving computers a sense they've been missing that's tied very directly to human well-being.

r001.rationale: The response mentions early diagnostics as a potential application, but does not propose disease detection as a benchmark.

r002.rationale: It describes formulating a physical scent recipe, but does not propose scented consumer-product development as a benchmark.

r003.rationale: It envisions smell as another modality in larger models, but does not say smell capability should be explicitly evaluated in general-purpose foundation models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that smell is the one sense that we really haven't digitized yet. We have cameras, we have microphones, and that's why vision and language models have had so much to learn from, there are just oceans of data. There's no equivalent for smell. So when I think about building olfaction into foundation models, the honest answer is that the model is almost the easier part. The hard part is creating the sensor and the data that let the model learn anything at all.

The way we've approached it at Osmo is to start with the structure of a molecule as the input, because in the end, smell is chemistry. Every odor you've ever experienced is a set of molecules binding to receptors in your nose. So you can take a graph neural network, feed it a molecular structure, and train it to predict how a human would describe that smell, things like musky, floral, grassy, meaty. What was surprising to us is that this works, and it works about as well as a trained human panelist. The model learns an embedding space where molecules that smell alike end up close together even when their chemical structures look completely different. That embedding is really the beginning of a map of odor, something that just didn't exist before.

Now, that's a single-modality model. The question you're asking is how this becomes part of a foundation model in the sense that people mean it today. I think the path there is the same one that vision took when it joined language. You need a representation for smell that can be aligned with text and with other sensory data. If I have an embedding for "the smell of fresh-cut grass," and I have the text for it, and maybe an image of a lawn, those can start to live in a shared space. Once you have that, a model can reason about smell the way it currently reasons about what's in a photo.

But the bottleneck, again, is data. The world has maybe a few thousand molecules that have been smelled and described carefully by humans. Compare that to billions of captioned images. So part of our work has been building the hardware side, sensors that can actually read a scent out of the air and turn it into a signal a model can use, and then the other direction, the ability to take a digital representation of a smell and physically reproduce it. You need the full loop: read the scent, represent it, and write it back out. When you can do that, you can collect data at a scale that was never possible before, and that's when I think olfaction stops being a niche project and becomes a genuine modality inside these large models.

And I'd say the reason to do it isn't just that it would be cool to have a computer that can smell. The nose is an incredibly sensitive chemical detector. It gives us a route into disease detection, food safety, environmental monitoring, things where we're currently blind because our machines don't have this sense. So giving computers a sense of smell is really about giving them access to a whole layer of information about the physical world that they've been missing.

r001.rationale: Disease detection is named as a possible application, but the response does not propose it as a benchmark for a smell-enabled foundation model.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention scented consumer-product development as an application or benchmark.

r003.rationale: The response says olfaction could become a modality inside large models, but does not propose explicitly evaluating smell as a dimension of general-purpose foundation models.

astra-6.text:
I think the first step is to give smell a representation that a model can work with. For language, we have tokens. For images, we have pixels. With smell, you have molecules, but the relationship between a molecule’s structure and what you perceive isn’t straightforward. And most things we smell are mixtures, which makes that problem even more interesting.

So I’d start by learning a representation that connects molecular structure to human perception—a kind of map where proximity tells you something about how similar two things smell. Then you can begin connecting that representation to language, images, and other modalities. When you say “a rose,” the model could connect the word and the visual appearance to an actual representation of its scent.

But the crucial piece is grounding. There’s a difference between a model that can write a convincing description of a smell and one that can predict what a new molecule or mixture will smell like. To get there, we need measurements, human sensory data, and experiments that test those predictions. That’s how smell becomes more than another thing a model can talk about—it becomes something the model can reason about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predicting smells and testing predictions, but does not propose disease detection as a benchmark.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention scented consumer-product development as a benchmark.

r003.rationale: It calls for measurements, sensory data, and experiments, but does not say smell should be an explicitly evaluated dimension of general-purpose foundation models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is to give smell a representation that a model can actually work with. With language, we have tokens. With images, we have pixels. For smell, we need a way to connect the structure of a molecule to what someone actually perceives when they smell it.

Then you can imagine connecting that representation to language and vision. If you show a model a picture of a forest, it might describe what you would see and hear. We'd like it to also understand what you might smell—the pine needles, the soil, the damp leaves—and connect that description to actual molecules.

The challenge is getting the grounding right. A model can talk fluently about the smell of a rose without understanding which molecules produce that experience. So I envision building toward foundation models that connect chemistry, perception, and language, where smell becomes another modality that the model can reason across.

r001.rationale: The response discusses linking molecular chemistry to smell perception, but does not propose disease detection as a benchmark.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention scented consumer-product development as a benchmark.

r003.rationale: It describes smell as another modality for foundation models, but does not say that smell capability should be an explicitly evaluated dimension.
